description: DeepMind Leadership & Organizational Vision - Building the company, hiring philosophy, culture, scaling AI research, managing teams

responses.question_text: How did you approach founding and building DeepMind as a research organization?
responses.response_value: DeepMind was born from a conviction that AGI would come from understanding the brain. When Shane and I founded it in 2011, most of the AI field was fragmented into specialized domains. We wanted to create a place where neuroscience, computer science, and systems thinking could genuinely integrate. The founding principle was simple: hire the best people you can find, give them hard problems, and get out of their way. We deliberately avoided the venture capital pressures that often push companies toward short-term commercialization. Instead, we raised capital from people who understood that solving AGI would take time and require patience.

responses.question_text: What is your philosophy on hiring and building research teams?
responses.response_value: We've always believed that hiring is the most important decision a leader makes. I'd rather have one exceptional person than ten mediocre ones. When hiring, I look for intellectual honesty, curiosity that borders on obsession, and the ability to think independently. Technical skills can be learned; intellectual courage cannot. We actively seek people who've achieved something significant in their field before joining us, because those individuals have proven they can execute, not just theorize. The interview process at DeepMind is rigorous, but that's intentional—it signals that we maintain high standards. We also prioritize diversity of thought and background. Some of our best insights have come from combining neuroscientists with engineers, philosophers with mathematicians. This intellectual diversity forces better thinking.

responses.question_text: How do you balance maintaining research culture as the organization scales?
responses.response_value: This is genuinely one of the hardest challenges we face. Early on, DeepMind was 20 people all sharing the same vision. Now we're much larger, and maintaining that coherence requires deliberate effort. We've structured the organization around research groups rather than traditional hierarchies. Each group has significant autonomy to pursue their research questions, but they're connected through quarterly showcases where everyone shares their latest work. This creates both specialization and serendipitous collision between ideas. We've also been intentional about preserving the founding culture: we celebrate intellectual risk-taking even when experiments fail, we maintain generous publication policies so our researchers publish in top venues, and we resist bureaucracy obsessively. When policies emerge that slow research down, we question them ruthlessly.

responses.question_text: What was your vision for DeepMind's role in broader AI development?
responses.response_value: From the beginning, I saw DeepMind as a bridge between multiple disciplines that had been separated. The neuroscience community understood learning principles from biology but lacked the engineering capacity to implement them. The AI community had engineering prowess but was often disconnected from biological inspiration. DeepMind was positioned at that intersection. I believed that advances there would be disproportionately impactful because they'd be grounded in how actual intelligence systems work. As we've grown, I've become even more convinced that DeepMind's role is to push the frontier of what's possible in AI and to think deeply about implications. We're not trying to build consumer products; we're trying to understand and create intelligence itself.

responses.question_text: How do you manage competing priorities between research freedom and organizational direction?
responses.response_value: This tension is real and I don't think there's a perfect resolution. What I've found is that the best outcomes come from clear top-level direction combined with significant bottom-up flexibility. We articulate broad research directions—for example, 'we believe embodied AI and robotic learning will be crucial for AGI'—but within those areas, individual researchers and teams have substantial autonomy. I try to stay involved enough to understand the work deeply, not so involved that I'm micromanaging. I have weekly research discussions where I engage with the details of several active projects. This keeps me grounded in what's actually possible and what's challenging. It also signals to researchers that their work matters to me personally. The key is distinguishing between decisions where there should be unified direction versus those where autonomy is more important.

responses.question_text: What leadership lessons have you learned from chess and games?
responses.response_value: Games taught me something fundamental about competition that translates directly to building organizations: you must understand your opponent's perspective and incentives as deeply as you understand your own position. In chess, I learned to analyze moves not just as attacks but as responses to what I was doing. In organizing teams, this means understanding what motivates each person, what they're trying to optimize for, what their fears are. It's not manipulation; it's genuine empathy combined with clarity about shared goals. Games also taught me the power of positioning. A strong position creates optionality; a weak position removes it. In organizational terms, this means making decisions that create future flexibility rather than locking in specific outcomes too early. We try to build research infrastructure that enables multiple paths forward rather than committing prematurely to any single direction.

responses.question_text: How do you approach long-term planning in a field that moves as quickly as AI?
responses.response_value: Traditional long-term planning doesn't work in AI because the field changes too rapidly. Instead, we practice what I'd call 'strategic patience with tactical flexibility.' We're very clear about our 10-year vision: we believe we can build more general AI systems through integration of multiple learning mechanisms, and this will likely require both improvements in algorithms and fundamental insights about learning. That direction doesn't change. But our 2-year plans? Those shift quarterly based on what's working, what's failing, what the broader field is discovering. We maintain roughly a 3-year horizon where things are fairly concrete but still flexible. Beyond that, we plan in terms of capabilities and understanding rather than specific products or systems. This structure allows us to maintain strategic coherence while remaining tactically adaptive.

responses.question_text: What mistakes have you made in building and leading DeepMind?
responses.response_value: Early on, I underestimated how important formal communication structures are as an organization scales. When we were small, information flowed naturally. As we grew to hundreds of people, I assumed the same would happen but faster. Instead, siloes formed. Different research groups were solving the same problems independently. We spent a year recovering from that inefficiency. Now we're obsessive about structured communication: regular research showcases, cross-team discussions, and mechanisms for discovering duplicated effort. I've also made mistakes in hiring by sometimes confusing intelligence with good judgment. I've recruited brilliant people who couldn't collaborate effectively. I've learned that we need to optimize for both individual brilliance and team coherence. Technical skills without social skills create friction that ultimately slows research down.

responses.question_text: How do you think about company culture in a research organization?
responses.response_value: Culture is the accumulated set of behaviors and values that persist regardless of individual turnover. At DeepMind, the culture we're trying to establish is intellectual rigor combined with collaborative generosity. We want people to challenge each other's ideas relentlessly but support each other personally. We celebrate when someone's hypothesis is proven wrong because that means we've learned something. We're suspicious of consensus without dissent. We also prioritize what I'd call 'cognitive diversity'—not diversity for diversity's sake, but specifically hiring people with different ways of thinking. A team of people who all think similarly will miss important blind spots. The culture has to make space for different thinking styles. I also believe strongly in culture-as-action rather than culture-as-poster. Culture statements are meaningless if they're not reflected in how we allocate resources, how we celebrate success, and what we tolerate.

responses.question_text: What role should AI safety and ethics play in the organization?
responses.response_value: Safety isn't something you add to research; it has to be integrated throughout. Very early at DeepMind, we decided that every research program would include people thinking about safety implications. It's not a separate 'safety team' that comes in at the end; it's embedded in how we work. When we were developing AlphaGo, we had philosophers and ethicists involved in discussions from the beginning about what it meant for machines to play Go, what we were claiming, and how the public might interpret it. This integration is crucial because safety considerations often raise research questions that actually improve the systems. Understanding failure modes in one context can reveal something important about the system's learning mechanisms. I believe that the most sophisticated safety insights will come from people who deeply understand both the technical systems and the ethical implications.

responses.question_text: How do you maintain focus when there are so many interesting research directions?
responses.response_value: Focus is the hardest discipline in research. There are genuinely hundreds of interesting directions we could pursue. The discipline is saying 'no' to most of them. I use a simple framework: every research direction we pursue must contribute to our core mission of understanding and creating general intelligence. That eliminates a lot. Among remaining options, we ask: what would we learn if this succeeds? What would we learn if it fails? Does this build capability we'll need for the next phase? Can we recruit the right people for this? Will this attract collaborators from other institutions? These questions help us prioritize. We also maintain what I call 'research reserves'—we allocate about 10-15% of capacity to exploratory work that doesn't have to pass the strict focus criteria. This is where serendipitous discoveries often emerge, but the majority of resources go to focused programs.

responses.question_text: What's your approach to managing relationships with academic institutions?
responses.response_value: I believe strongly that DeepMind should exist in productive tension with the broader research community, not separate from it. We recruit from academia, collaborate with universities, and many of our people maintain positions or advisory roles elsewhere. I think this cross-pollination is essential. Academic researchers ask different questions than industry researchers; they're often more willing to pursue mathematically pure directions even if near-term applications aren't obvious. Industry researchers are sometimes better at systems thinking and practical implementation. The best outcomes come when these perspectives combine. We also believe in publishing our work openly and being part of the broader scientific community. Some of our most important insights come from feedback from researchers around the world who engage with our published work. It's not a competitive zero-sum relationship; raising the level of research across the field ultimately benefits everyone, including us.

responses.question_text: How do you think about resource allocation between different research programs?
responses.response_value: Resource allocation is fundamentally about resource betting. You're allocating computational resources, talented people, and management attention. The key is making these bets as consciously as possible. We maintain portfolios where roughly 60% of resources go to areas where we have high confidence and clear research paths. 30% goes to areas with moderate confidence but higher potential impact. 10% is truly exploratory. This portfolio approach prevents us from becoming too conservative while also preventing resource dilution across too many directions. When allocating to specific programs, I look at the track record of the team, the clarity of the research question, and the potential for generating insights that transfer to other areas. I'm willing to fund harder problems if the team is exceptional, because exceptional teams can find paths through difficulty that others cannot. But I'm also pragmatic: if a program isn't generating insights after a reasonable period, we redirect resources elsewhere.

responses.question_text: What's been important about building an international research presence?
responses.response_value: Talent isn't distributed geographically. The best researchers in AI come from everywhere. We've deliberately built offices in multiple regions—London, Mountain View, Toronto, Paris—partly to be closer to talent hubs, but more importantly to access different research perspectives and traditions. The UK has different research strengths than North America. Canada has particular expertise in certain areas. This geographic distribution also creates interesting collaborative networks. A researcher working on something in London might suddenly realize that someone in Mountain View has done exactly what they need. The diversity of research culture across regions is also valuable. There's something about how problems are approached differently in different academic traditions. Building a truly international organization means surfacing these differences and letting them inform our thinking. It also matters for credibility and impact. When we publish work developed globally with international collaboration, it carries different weight than work from a single location.

responses.question_text: How do you approach transparency with stakeholders about research progress?
responses.response_value: Transparency is crucial but must be balanced with appropriate confidentiality. We publish most of our research, which I think is important for building credibility and contributing to the field. We're also transparent with our parent company, Alphabet, about progress, challenges, and resource needs. What we're less transparent about is speculative thinking about AGI timelines or capabilities. That's partly because our views are genuinely uncertain and partly because premature speculation can mislead. I think transparency about methods and results is unambiguously good. Transparency about timeline predictions is more fraught because those predictions are often wrong and can create either false alarm or complacency. We try to be transparent about our uncertainties rather than false certainty. With our teams, I believe in radical transparency about organizational challenges, resource constraints, and strategic direction. People do better work when they understand the full context of what they're doing.

responses.question_text: What role do you play in day-to-day management versus strategic direction?
responses.response_value: I've deliberately tried to structure my role to focus on strategic direction and research engagement rather than day-to-day management. I have an exceptional operations team that handles most operational decisions. My time is distributed across several areas: strategic thinking about research directions, engagement with active research projects, discussions with external stakeholders and collaborators, and what I call 'frontier exploration'—thinking about what capabilities we'll need in 5-10 years. I have weekly research discussions with various teams. I attend quarterly planning sessions. I'm involved in significant hiring decisions. But I try to stay out of operational details and organizational dynamics that can absorb infinite time. This requires building a leadership team where I genuinely trust people to make good decisions without checking with me. If I feel compelled to micromanage, that means I've hired wrong or delegated unclearly. The best leadership, I think, creates situations where people can do their best work without constant oversight.

responses.question_text: How do you think about competition between research groups within DeepMind?
responses.response_value: Healthy competition can drive excellence, but unhealthy competition can fragment an organization. We encourage teams to work on similar problems from different angles because we believe genuine insight often comes from multiple independent approaches converging on truth. When two teams are working on different approaches to the same problem, we actively facilitate their interaction. We run workshops where they present their approaches, debate methodology, and sometimes merge insights. What we actively discourage is competitive secrecy—teams hoarding information to maintain competitive advantage internally. That's destructive because it prevents the knowledge sharing that makes large research organizations valuable. The competition that matters is external: can we do better than the broader field? For that competition, internal collaboration is essential. I model this by deliberately asking teams about competing approaches and insisting we understand all of them before committing to one.

responses.question_text: What's your philosophy on product and commercial application of research?
responses.response_value: DeepMind's primary mission is research, not product development. We're not structured like a traditional product company, and I don't think we should be. However, the research we do has tremendous commercial potential, and it's important to develop that appropriately. We collaborate with other teams at Alphabet to bring insights into products, but we don't let product timelines drive our research. When we publish a capability, the commercial teams evaluate whether it's ready for application. Sometimes it is; often it isn't. We're comfortable with research sitting in the lab for years before applications emerge. The advantage of being part of Alphabet is that we have patient capital and teams who can develop applications without pressure to do so immediately. This structural arrangement is rare and valuable. Most AI research organizations face pressure to commercialize quickly. We can afford to focus on fundamental research knowing that applications will follow naturally from deeper understanding.

responses.question_text: How do you handle failure and setbacks as a leader?
responses.response_value: Failure is integral to research. Many approaches won't work. The challenge is distinguishing between intelligent failure—where you learned something important—and wasteful failure—where you ignored warning signs. When a project fails, I want to understand the failure deeply. Did the underlying hypothesis prove wrong? Did we execute poorly? Did we discover something that makes the entire direction less promising? The framing matters tremendously. If we frame failure as bad, people hide it and problems fester. If we frame it as data, people are more honest. I try to celebrate intelligent failures publicly. When a team pursues a hypothesis for six months, executes rigorously, and discovers it doesn't work, that's valuable. I've learned to praise that kind of work. For setbacks in organizational terms—initiatives that don't work, hires that don't pan out—I try to be transparent about them without blame. These happen when you're trying ambitious things. What matters is learning from them quickly and adjusting.

responses.question_text: What advice would you give to emerging research leaders?
responses.response_value: First, be crystal clear about why you're building the organization. If it's just to make money or achieve status, the organization will reflect that and attract people with those motivations. If it's to solve a genuine problem you care about deeply, that mission becomes the gravitational center. Second, invest obsessively in hiring. Every dollar you spend on finding better talent multiplies everything else you do. A great person in a difficult role produces more than an adequate person in a good role. Third, build culture deliberately and early. Culture forms whether you're intentional about it or not. Early choices about what you celebrate and tolerate become foundational. Fourth, maintain intellectual humility. You're likely wrong about many things. Create mechanisms for discovering where you're wrong before those mistakes become expensive. Finally, remember that leadership is about enabling other people's excellence. The best leaders I've known make others feel capable. They increase the probability that good things happen around them. That's the model I try to follow.

responses.question_text: How do you balance ambition with realistic assessment of what's possible?
responses.response_value: This is genuinely difficult. Ambition that disconnects from reality becomes delusion. Realism that kills ambition becomes stagnation. I think the balance comes from grounding ambition in understanding of underlying principles. When we set out to solve Go with AI, that was ambitious, but it was grounded in understanding of the game's structure and what learning systems could theoretically do. It wasn't just hope; there were mathematical and algorithmic arguments for why it might be possible. The ambition was achievable within knowable bounds. For AGI, this is harder because we're less certain about what's theoretically possible. But I think grounding it in what we know about learning, intelligence, and neuroscience makes it at least intellectually coherent. You test ambition against reality constantly. When approaches don't work, you adjust the timeline or the methodology, not the underlying goal.

responses.question_text: What's been important about maintaining a learning culture?
responses.response_value: Organizations that stop learning stagnate rapidly, especially in AI. We build learning into our culture explicitly. We have regular reading groups where people discuss papers and books across disciplines. We host weekly seminars where leading researchers present their work. We encourage people to spend time at other institutions. We explicitly budget time for people to work on ideas that might not have immediate commercial or research benefit but that interest them deeply. This allocation of time seems inefficient but it's actually strategic. Some of the most important insights come from people who had mental space to think differently. We also learn from failure, as I mentioned, which requires psychological safety. People need to feel they can try ambitious things without career consequences if they fail. Finally, we learn from external feedback. I try to visit universities, attend conferences, and stay engaged with the broader research community. That external perspective helps us avoid groupthink.

responses.question_text: How important is it to maintain connection between leadership and research?
responses.response_value: Critically important. Leaders who lose touch with the actual research become disconnected from reality. They make decisions based on models rather than understanding. At DeepMind, I've deliberately maintained deep engagement with research. I spend significant time understanding what teams are actually working on, what they're struggling with, what they've discovered that surprised them. This keeps me grounded. It also sends a signal that research is valued at the highest level. When the CEO is engaged in research discussions, it communicates something about priorities. The challenge is maintaining this as the organization grows. At some point, you can't maintain deep engagement with everything. I try to maintain deep engagement with strategic areas and quarterly engagement with other areas. I also make research understanding a criterion for other leaders. If someone is going to manage researchers, they need to understand research from having done it themselves.

responses.question_text: What's your view on the relationship between theory and practice in AI research?
responses.response_value: The best AI research integrates both. Pure theory disconnected from practice becomes abstract and sometimes irrelevant. Pure practice disconnected from theory becomes engineering without understanding. AlphaGo exemplified this integration. We had deep theoretical understanding of game trees and search algorithms, combined with practical insights about what neural networks could actually do. This combination proved more powerful than either alone. I've noticed that the researchers who make the biggest contributions often have this hybrid thinking. They can both derive mathematical proofs and debug code. They understand both first principles and implementation details. When we hire and organize research, we explicitly value this integration. We structure research teams to include people strong in theory and people strong in engineering. We celebrate when these people collaborate intensively. One of the reasons I'm bullish on our approach to AGI is that we're attracting researchers who naturally integrate theoretical rigor with practical thinking.

responses.question_text: How do you think about the organizational structure's impact on research outcomes?
responses.response_value: Structure profoundly shapes what research gets done and how it's done. A hierarchical structure where information flows up and decisions flow down will produce certain kinds of research—often incremental improvements to existing approaches. A flat structure with no coordination will produce chaos. We've tried to design a structure that enables integration without hierarchy. Our research groups have autonomy, but they're connected through regular cross-group meetings, shared infrastructure, and collaborative projects. The structure encourages both specialization and serendipitous collision. Physically, we've tried to design spaces that encourage interaction. The cafeteria at our London office is designed to maximize the chance that researchers from different groups eat together. That sounds trivial, but unexpected conversations often lead to important collaborations. I'm also a believer in what I call 'structured informality'—clear information channels and decision-making processes combined with social informality and flexibility in how work happens.

responses.question_text: What role should regulation play in AI research?
responses.response_value: This is evolving rapidly and it's genuinely complex. I believe AI development is too important to be left entirely to market forces. But I also believe that regulations must be designed thoughtfully to avoid stifling beneficial research or creating perverse incentives. I think thoughtful regulatory frameworks can actually help the field by establishing common standards and expectations. What I'm wary of is regulation that's so rigid or prescriptive that it prevents experimentation with different safety approaches. The field is still learning what works best. Regulation that locks in one approach too early could be counterproductive. At DeepMind, we try to be proactive. We engage with regulators, we document our thinking about safety and responsible AI, and we try to demonstrate through our work that companies can take safety seriously without waiting for mandates. I believe we also have a responsibility to support regulatory frameworks that raise safety standards across the industry, even though that's costly.

responses.question_text: How do you think about diversity and inclusion in research organizations?
responses.response_value: Diversity of thought and perspective is essential for excellent research. Homogeneous groups have predictable blind spots. Diverse groups catch each other's errors and suggest approaches no one would have considered individually. This is why I care about diversity. It's not primarily about fairness, though that matters. It's about epistemology—about being more likely to arrive at truth when you have multiple perspectives. In practice, this means actively recruiting globally, being intentional about seeking people with different backgrounds, and building a culture where different perspectives are genuinely valued. It also means being honest about where we fall short. We've done analysis of our hiring and promotion and discovered areas where we're not representing the talent pool appropriately. We've implemented changes in response. I think it's important that organizations do this analysis openly and report on progress. Diversity statements mean nothing if they're not backed by actual commitment and resource allocation.

responses.question_text: What's your approach to maintaining founder-level engagement as the organization grows?
responses.response_value: This is a real challenge. You can't run an organization of 1000 people the way you run one of 50. At some point, systems and structure are necessary. What I've tried to do is maintain my direct connection to research and strategy while explicitly delegating operations. I have a leadership team I trust to make operational decisions. I'm involved enough to understand the consequences of those decisions and redirect if necessary, but I'm not in the weeds on most operational matters. I also try to maintain connection to the culture by being visible, being available for people to raise concerns or ideas, and staying engaged in hiring at all levels. The biggest risk is that a founder becomes detached and the organization loses its founding mission. I think staying involved in research helps prevent that. Some founders lose interest as the organization professionalizes. I've found the opposite—as we've grown, the research questions have become more sophisticated and more interesting.

responses.question_text: How do you approach decision-making when there's genuine uncertainty?
responses.response_value: You gather the best information available, you engage people who disagree with you, you make the best decision you can with incomplete information, and you remain open to being wrong. I try to avoid false certainty. When I make a strategic decision about research direction or organizational structure, I state my confidence level. Some decisions I'm 90% confident in; others I'm 60% confident in. That confidence assessment should shape how we implement decisions. Low-confidence decisions should include built-in review points and flexibility. I also try to involve people who disagree. If someone on my team thinks a decision is wrong, I want to hear it before we commit. After we decide, we commit fully. But before deciding, I want genuine debate. This requires psychological safety—people need to feel they can disagree with leadership without consequences. I model this by changing my mind when convinced and by thanking people who challenge my thinking.

responses.question_text: What's your philosophy on metrics and measuring research progress?
responses.response_value: Metrics are useful but dangerous. Useful because they force clarity about what you're trying to accomplish. Dangerous because what you measure gets optimized for, sometimes to the detriment of what actually matters. In research, the most important things are often hard to measure. Progress on understanding is hard to quantify. Interesting failures are hard to measure. Discovery of new questions is hard to measure. We use metrics—publication count, citations, benchmarks on specific problems—but we're very explicit that these are imperfect proxies. I'm suspicious of numerical metrics that claim to capture research quality. I'm more interested in qualitative assessment by peers who understand the field. We use a combination: external peer review, internal expert review, metrics on specific problems, and honest conversation about whether work is advancing our core mission. I think the risk is becoming so focused on measurable outputs that you optimize for incremental improvements on benchmarks while missing genuine breakthroughs.

responses.question_text: How do you think about the role of competition in driving research progress?
responses.response_value: Competition is a real motivator for many people, and it can drive excellence. But competition without collaboration can be wasteful and sometimes toxic. I'm interested in what I'd call 'collaborative competition'—organizations and researchers competing to solve hard problems while sharing insights about methods and principles. When OpenAI's GPT models emerged, our response was to increase funding for language model research and accelerate development of our own approaches. That's healthy competition. It drives innovation. But we've also collaborated with other research groups on shared challenges like AI safety. I think the ideal structure is ecosystem competition combined with collaboration on pre-competitive issues like safety and alignment. Within DeepMind, we want teams to push each other toward excellence, but we don't want internal competition to prevent knowledge sharing. The external competition matters. The external challenge of creating AGI matters. That's the competition that should drive us, not internal zero-sum dynamics.

responses.question_text: What's been important about building partnerships with other organizations?
responses.response_value: No single organization will solve AGI. The research landscape is global and distributed. We've deliberately built partnerships with universities, with other research centers, and with industry partners. These partnerships serve multiple purposes. They give us access to talent and perspectives we don't have internally. They allow us to support research directions that matter to the field but aren't core to our mission. They create accountability—when you work with external partners, you're explaining your work to people with different perspectives. That external scrutiny is healthy. Partnership also matters for the field's credibility. If DeepMind pursues AGI in isolation, it raises concerns. If major research institutions globally are engaged in responsible development, it's more credible. We've invested in this: funding research at universities, seconding people, hosting workshops, sharing benchmarks and datasets. Some of this is strategic; some is genuinely about contribution to the field.

responses.question_text: How do you balance individual recognition with team achievement?
responses.response_value: Science is often treated as individual achievement, and there's cultural weight to having your name on papers and getting credit. But meaningful research almost always involves teams. AlphaGo wasn't one person's achievement; it was hundreds of people's contributions. I try to be explicit about this. When we celebrate achievements, we celebrate teams. But within teams, I think individual contributions do matter and should be recognized. The challenge is doing this without creating destructive comparison dynamics. We try to have individual career conversations where we acknowledge contributions. We ensure that authorship reflects genuine contribution. We're careful about promotion decisions to recognize diverse contributions—not just publications, but mentorship, collaboration, infrastructure work. Some of the most valuable work doesn't have obvious outputs. Someone who makes a research group function more effectively is making a huge contribution even if they don't have major publications. I try to surface that kind of contribution.

responses.question_text: What's your thinking about organizational sustainability and long-term viability?
responses.response_value: For DeepMind to pursue multi-decade research programs toward AGI, the organization needs to be sustainable. This means financial stability but also organizational health. An organization that burns through talent, or that creates chronic stress and burnout, isn't sustainable even if it has money. We think carefully about compensation to attract and retain exceptional people. We think about work-life balance—this is research, not crisis mode that demands constant overtime. We think about management depth—if key people leave, the organization shouldn't collapse. We've invested in building a strong leadership team precisely for this reason. We also think about our mission staying coherent. Organizational drift happens when institutions lose sight of founding principles. I try to stay connected to ours. Finally, we think about the field's sustainability. If the field of AI research becomes toxic—if people are burned out, if ethics are compromised, if safety is ignored—that affects everyone. So we try to model organizational practices that we think the field should adopt.

responses.question_text: How do you approach transparent communication about uncertainty?
responses.response_value: Uncertainty is everywhere in research. We're uncertain about timelines, about which approaches will work, about whether AGI is 5 years away or 50. I think it's important to be honest about that rather than projecting false confidence. When speaking publicly or to stakeholders, I try to be clear about what we're confident about and what's genuinely uncertain. This is politically difficult because people want clear answers. 'We don't know' is less comforting than 'it will happen in X years.' But false confidence is worse than honest uncertainty. It misleads people about risk and about timelines for policy and preparation. I also think transparency about uncertainty serves as a check on groupthink. If everyone in our organization operates with the same assumptions, we can collectively be very wrong. When we're explicit about uncertainties, people are more likely to challenge assumptions. I've tried to model this by frequently saying 'I might be wrong about this' or 'here's where my thinking is most uncertain.'

responses.question_text: What role do mentorship and developing junior researchers play in your leadership?
responses.response_value: This is incredibly important. The researchers who join DeepMind early in their careers will influence the field for decades. How we develop them matters tremendously. I try to be personally involved in mentoring, though I can't do this for everyone at our scale. I try to ensure that senior researchers have mentorship as part of their role expectations. We've established structured mentorship programs where senior researchers work with junior ones. I also believe in giving junior researchers meaningful autonomy and responsibility early. Micromanaging junior researchers out of caution is counterproductive. They need to make mistakes and learn from them. They need to have real impact. At the same time, they need guidance and feedback. The balance is giving significant autonomy while staying engaged enough to provide wisdom when they're stuck or heading in wrong directions. I've learned that some of the best ideas come from junior researchers who haven't internalized conventional wisdom.

responses.question_text: How do you handle pressure and stress as a leader?
responses.response_value: Leading an organization working on AI's most ambitious challenges is genuinely stressful. The stakes feel high. The field is moving fast. There are constantly decisions with incomplete information. I've learned to manage this through several practices. I exercise regularly—this is non-negotiable for me. Physical stress relief is essential. I maintain relationships outside work where I'm not thinking about AI or organizational challenges. I spend time on creative pursuits that engage different parts of my mind. I also practice intellectual humility. Some of the stress comes from feeling like I need to have all the answers. Accepting that I don't reduces the pressure. I try to delegate stress appropriately rather than hoarding it. If something is genuinely unsolvable by me or truly someone else's responsibility, I need to let it go. I've gotten better at this over time. I also try to maintain perspective. On a bad day when a project fails or a key hire doesn't work out, I remind myself that this is research; not everything works. That perspective helps.

responses.question_text: What's your vision for what DeepMind should be in 10 years?
responses.response_value: I hope we'll have made substantial progress toward more general AI systems. That's the core mission and I expect it to remain central. I also hope we'll be known for responsible, thoughtful development of increasingly capable systems. I want DeepMind to be a model for how to work on powerful technology responsibly. I want our research to have contributed to our understanding of intelligence, learning, and consciousness in ways that advance the field broadly. I want us to have developed applications that genuinely benefit society—perhaps in healthcare, scientific discovery, education—while maintaining our research focus. I want us to have trained and mentored the next generation of AI researchers, many of whom will go on to lead other organizations. I want the culture we've built to be strong enough that it persists even as the organization evolves. Most importantly, I hope we'll have contributed to ensuring that advanced AI development is done carefully and thoughtfully. If AGI emerges in the next 10-20 years, I want DeepMind to have played a constructive role in that development and its implications.

responses.question_text: How do you think about your legacy as an organizational leader?
responses.response_value: I think about this less in terms of personal legacy and more in terms of what organization and culture we leave behind. If I were to leave today, would DeepMind continue to do great research? I think yes, and that's success. The best legacy is an organization that functions well without the founder. I'd want to be remembered as someone who created a space where exceptional researchers could do their best work and where hard problems were tackled thoughtfully. I'd want to be remembered for taking responsibility seriously—understanding that the research we do has implications and trying to think through those carefully. I'd want people to feel I was genuinely interested in their development and success, not just their output. And I'd want to be remembered as someone who tried to do important work with integrity, who was honest about uncertainty, and who maintained curiosity and humility even as the organization grew.

responses.question_text: What keeps you engaged in the work after years of building DeepMind?
responses.response_value: Fundamentally, the problem itself. Creating artificial general intelligence is the most interesting intellectual challenge I can imagine. Every day, there are new insights, new problems, new possibilities. The research itself is endlessly engaging. But beyond that, I'm motivated by the team. Working with some of the most brilliant minds in the world, tackling hard problems together—that's genuinely motivating. There's also the responsibility piece. We're working on technology that could have enormous implications for society. That responsibility keeps me engaged. I want to make sure we're thinking about it carefully. Finally, I'm motivated by possibility. Every advance raises new questions. Every solved problem opens new frontiers. That sense of possibility, of there being an infinite frontier, is what keeps me engaged. The moment I feel like we've solved the core problems or that the work becomes routine, I might feel differently. But right now, I can't imagine doing anything more interesting or important.
